problem: It says a box shows one dot per free instance, so two held printers out of three leave one dot. This contradicts the bullet earlier in the same section (one dot per instance) and contradicts the standard graph model, where every instance always keeps its dot and an assignment edge starts at that dot when the instance is held. Under the chapter's own rule, a box with 3 instances and 2 held would wrongly appear to have only 1 instance.
fix: A box has one dot per instance, always, held or free. When an instance is held, the assignment edge starts at that dot and goes to the process. Three printers with two held still show three dots, with two assignment edges leaving two of them and one dot free.

problem: The second sentence, 'An unmarked or filled dot shows that instance is currently assigned', is garbled and wrong. Dots do not change appearance with allocation; allocation is shown only by an assignment edge leaving the dot.
fix: One dot is one instance of that resource type. Whether an instance is free or held is shown by the edges: if an assignment edge leaves a dot, that instance is held by the process it points to; a dot with no outgoing assignment edge is free.

problem: The second case, a process holding a lock that is never scheduled again while others wait, is labelled a deadlock. Under the chapter's own definition (a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another member of the set) and under the four conditions, this is indefinite blocking or starvation, not deadlock: the holder is not waiting for anything, so no circular wait exists. A student will carry away a wrong test for deadlock.
fix: Keep the first case as starvation. For the deadlock case, use a genuine cycle: process A holds lock L1 and waits for L2, process B holds L2 and waits for L1. Neither can proceed and neither will release, so the wait truly never ends.

where: Exam traps, last bullet (starvation is not deadlock)
problem: 'A deadlocked one cannot be helped by adding more of the same resource' is false. If two processes each hold one of two printers and each wants a second, adding a third printer lets one request be granted and the deadlock clears. Adding instances can break a deadlock; what cannot help is waiting longer.
fix: A starved process would finish once the resource reached it. A deadlocked process waits in a closed loop, so waiting longer never helps, though adding an extra instance of the contended resource type can sometimes break the cycle.

problem: 'Rust's borrow checker goes further and rejects some lock misuse at compile time' is wrong for lock-ordering deadlocks. Rust's compiler prevents data races through ownership; a lock-order deadlock between two threads compiles cleanly and hangs at run time.
fix: Rust's ownership rules rule out data races at compile time, but a lock-ordering deadlock between two threads still compiles and hangs at run time, so lock ordering is still the programmer's job.
